title: The Calvin Cycle: Fixing Carbon from Thin Air

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Where in a plant cell does the Calvin cycle run?
cards.back: In the stroma, the fluid inside the chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoid stacks.
cards.quote: The cycle runs in the stroma, the soup inside the chloroplast surrounding the thylakoid stacks.

cards.front: Why is "dark reactions" a misleading name for the Calvin cycle?
cards.back: It runs in daylight, and it cannot run without the light reactions, because it spends two of their products: ATP (energy) and NADPH (reducing power).
cards.quote: It runs in broad daylight, and it cannot run without the light reactions, because it spends two products they make

cards.front: In the Calvin cycle, the CO₂ acceptor is {{c1::RuBP}}, a five-carbon sugar; joining CO₂ to it makes the three-carbon acid 3-PGA.
cards.back: RuBP = ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate.
cards.quote: Meet the players: RuBP, a five-carbon sugar that accepts the CO₂; 3-PGA, the three-carbon acid the joining makes

cards.front: Algae are fed carbon-14-labeled CO₂ and killed after shorter and shorter exposures, and the labeled molecules are separated on paper. At the shortest exposures, where is most of the label, and what does that show?
cards.back: In 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA). Whatever is labeled first is the earliest product, so carbon from the air lands first in a three-carbon acid.
cards.quote: At the shortest exposures one spot held most of it: 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA).
cards.section: Act 1, the first clue: a three-carbon acid

cards.front: Why do leaves make Rubisco in such enormous amounts?
cards.back: Each active site in a typical plant Rubisco fixes only about 3 CO₂ per second, so plants compensate with quantity, up to about half of a leaf's soluble protein.
cards.quote: Rubisco is the most abundant protein on Earth, yet each active site in a typical plant enzyme fixes only about 3 CO2 per second.

cards.front: Three RuBP and three CO₂ enter the Calvin cycle. Count the carbons: how many three-carbon molecules form, how many trioses can the plant keep, and where do the rest go?
cards.back: 3 × 5 + 3 = 18 C → 6 3-PGA (18 C) → 6 trioses. One triose (3 C) leaves as profit; 5 trioses (15 C) are rebuilt into 3 RuBP (15 C).
cards.why: The profit equals exactly the three carbons that came from the air.
cards.quote: Only one triose is profit: three carbons, exactly as many as came from the air.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: The Calvin cycle's fixation enzyme, {{c1::Rubisco}}, joins one CO₂ to one RuBP.
cards.back: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, the most abundant protein on Earth.
cards.quote: Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase), the most abundant protein on Earth, joins one CO₂ to one RuBP (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate).
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Why does Rubisco's carboxylation of RuBP spend no ATP and no NADPH?
cards.back: No ATP: the reaction is strongly downhill on its own. No NADPH: no outside electrons enter; Rubisco shuffles electrons within the molecule. The energy is paid later.
cards.quote: It needs no ATP because the reaction is strongly downhill on its own, and no NADPH because no outside electrons enter
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Name the two enzymes of the Calvin cycle's reduction stage and what each spends.
cards.back: Phosphoglycerate kinase spends ATP to make 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate from 3-PGA; G3P dehydrogenase spends NADPH to reduce it to G3P, a triose.
cards.quote: Each 3-PGA is primed by ATP (phosphoglycerate kinase adds a phosphate to its acid end) to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, then reduced by NADPH
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: The Calvin cycle's two reduction steps are glycolysis's two steps run {{c1::backward}}, using NADPH instead of NADH.
cards.quote: These are glycolysis's two steps run backward, using NADPH instead of NADH.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Calvin-cycle regeneration turns five trioses (15 C) into {{c1::three five-carbon sugars}} (15 C), adding and losing no carbon.
cards.quote: The job is to turn five trioses (15 C) into three five-carbon sugars (15 C), adding and losing no carbon.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: In Calvin-cycle regeneration, what do aldolase and transketolase each do?
cards.back: Aldolase joins two sugars into one. Transketolase moves a two-carbon piece from one sugar to another.
cards.quote: Aldolase joins two sugars into one; transketolase moves a two-carbon piece from one sugar to another
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: In Calvin-cycle regeneration, transketolase moves two carbons from a six-carbon sugar onto a triose. What sizes are the two products, and how many trioses does the full four-step shuffle consume?
cards.back: 6 + 3 → 4 + 5 (9 carbons either side). Trioses used: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5, giving three five-carbon sugars (15 C).
cards.quote: Trioses used: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5; out come three five-carbon sugars, 15 carbons.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: What does phosphoribulokinase (PRK) do in the Calvin cycle, and what does it cost?
cards.back: It phosphorylates ribulose-5-phosphate to RuBP, the CO₂ acceptor, closing the loop. One ATP per RuBP; regeneration spends no NADPH.
cards.quote: Finally, phosphoribulokinase (PRK) spends one ATP on each to make RuBP, closing the loop.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Why does the ordinary C3 Calvin cycle at steady state spend ATP and NADPH in a 3:2 ratio per CO₂?
cards.back: Two kinds of step spend ATP, only one spends NADPH. Each CO₂ makes two 3-PGA (1 ATP + 1 NADPH each) and uses one RuBP (1 ATP at PRK): 2 × (1 + 1) + 1 = 3 ATP + 2 NADPH.
cards.quote: Two kinds of step spend ATP and only one spends NADPH
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: How does carbon's oxidation state confirm that fixing one CO₂ into sugar needs two NADPH?
cards.back: CO₂ carbon is at +4; sugar carbon averages 0. That takes at least four electrons per carbon, the load of two NADPH, by any route.
cards.quote: Turning CO₂ carbon (oxidation state +4, as oxidized as carbon gets) into sugar carbon (0 on average) takes at least four electrons per carbon
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: How much ATP and NADPH does the C3 Calvin cycle spend to make one hexose? Show the count.
cards.back: 6 CO₂ = 6 turns. 12 3-PGA reduced: 12 ATP + 12 NADPH. 6 RuBP rebuilt: 6 ATP. Total 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.
cards.quote: Six turns make 12 3-PGA: 12 ATP + 12 NADPH to reduce them.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: In the ordinary C3 cycle at steady state, how much ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle spend per G3P exported?
cards.back: One G3P = 3 CO₂. Reduction: 6 ATP + 6 NADPH. Regeneration: 3 ATP. Total 9 ATP + 6 NADPH.
cards.quote: Regeneration costs 3 ATP per three CO₂ and no NADPH.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Follow one fixed CO₂ carbon: which part of 3-PGA does it become, and what do ATP and NADPH turn it into?
cards.back: It becomes the acid (–COO⁻) end of one 3-PGA. ATP and NADPH turn that end into the aldehyde (C=O) end of G3P.
cards.why: Only one triose in six leaves per round, so the carbon may circle the loop several times before export.
cards.quote: Welded onto RuBP, it becomes the acid (–COO⁻) end of one 3-PGA, and ATP and NADPH turn that end into the aldehyde (C=O) end of a G3P.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: What happens to G3P exported from the Calvin cycle?
cards.back: Two trioses (one isomerized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate) join into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, then fructose-6-phosphate, closely mirroring gluconeogenesis (almost step for step). The plant then makes sucrose (exported via phloem) or starch (stored in the chloroplast).
cards.quote: The plant then makes sucrose, exported through the phloem, or starch, stockpiled in the chloroplast for the night.
cards.section: Count the carbons, and the bill follows

cards.front: Algae fixing labeled CO₂ steadily in the light are suddenly put in the dark. Predict what happens to the 3-PGA and RuBP pools, and why.
cards.back: 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls. Without ATP and NADPH, 3-PGA cannot be reduced, and RuBP cannot be rebuilt while Rubisco keeps using it.
cards.quote: 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls. Without ATP and NADPH, 3-PGA cannot be reduced
cards.section: Switch off the light, or the CO₂

cards.front: Algae fixing CO₂ in the light have their CO₂ supply cut off. Which pool rises, 3-PGA or RuBP, and what did this result identify?
cards.back: RuBP rises and 3-PGA falls: regeneration keeps making RuBP and nothing uses it. A molecule that piles up when CO₂ is withheld is a candidate acceptor, so this pointed to RuBP.
cards.why: Later confirmed with the purified enzyme.
cards.quote: A molecule that piles up when CO₂ is withheld is a candidate acceptor: this is the experiment that pointed to RuBP
cards.section: Switch off the light, or the CO₂

cards.front: Isolated chloroplasts in the light get ¹⁴CO₂, ample ATP and NADPH, and a drug that fully blocks phosphoribulokinase. Predict where the label collects and what happens to fixation.
cards.back: Label collects in 3-PGA and downstream sugar phosphates, then net fixation halts: ribulose-5-P cannot become RuBP, so the acceptor pool runs out.
cards.why: Rests on PRK making RuBP and the loop's weak point: without regeneration, fixation stops when RuBP runs out.
cards.quote: It also shows the loop's weak point: without regeneration, fixation stops when RuBP runs out.
cards.section: Switch off the light, or the CO₂

cards.front: Why must a chloroplast switch the Calvin cycle off at night?
cards.back: It would spend ATP and NADPH no longer being made. And because the chloroplast makes NADPH at night by burning sugar (oxidative pentose phosphate pathway), a running cycle would rebuild that sugar: a futile cycle.
cards.quote: so the cycle would build sugar while that pathway burns it: a futile cycle
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: Name the three stromal signals by which light switches on the Calvin cycle.
cards.back: Stromal pH rises from about 7 to 8; stromal Mg²⁺ rises (in the textbook account); and thioredoxin is reduced.
cards.quote: as the light reactions pump protons into the thylakoid lumen (the space inside the thylakoids), stromal pH rises from about 7 to 8.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: Rubisco interacts with two different CO₂ molecules. What does each one do?
cards.back: The activating CO₂ forms a carbamate on Lys-201 of the large subunit, which holds Mg²⁺ to build the active site. A different, substrate CO₂ is the one fixed onto RuBP.
cards.quote: So one CO₂ switches the enzyme on, and a different CO₂ gets fixed.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: How do the light-driven rise in stromal pH and (in the textbook account) Mg²⁺ activate Rubisco?
cards.back: High pH helps Lys-201 react with CO₂ to form the carbamate; more Mg²⁺ completes the carbamate–Mg²⁺ pair that builds the working active site.
cards.quote: High pH helps the lysine react, and more Mg²⁺ completes the pair.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: What does Rubisco activase do?
cards.back: It is an ATP-burning chaperone (an AAA+ ATPase) that pries RuBP loose from a Rubisco that was not switched on and has clamped onto it; it also strips inhibitory sugar phosphates such as CA1P.
cards.quote: A Rubisco that is not switched on clamps onto RuBP so tightly it shuts itself down, and an ATP-burning chaperone, Rubisco activase, pries the sugar loose.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: How does reduced thioredoxin switch on Calvin-cycle enzymes in the light?
cards.back: Photosystem I → reduced ferredoxin → ferredoxin-thioredoxin reductase → reduced thioredoxin. Thioredoxin breaks a regulatory S–S bridge into two –SH groups in FBPase, SBPase, PRK and chloroplast G3P dehydrogenase, letting each take its active shape.
cards.quote: thioredoxin reduces a regulatory disulfide, breaking an S–S bridge between two cysteines into two –SH groups so the enzyme can take its active shape.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: Chloroplasts are kept in the light, but a reagent re-oxidizes thioredoxin as fast as it is reduced. Predict which Calvin enzymes are affected and what happens to the cycle.
cards.back: FBPase, SBPase, PRK and chloroplast G3P dehydrogenase would be held largely oxidized and inactive, so the cycle would be expected to stall or slow despite the light.
cards.why: Activation requires thioredoxin to reduce those disulfides; re-oxidation reforms them.
cards.quote: At nightfall thioredoxin is re-oxidized via peroxiredoxin, which passes the electrons to hydrogen peroxide; the disulfides reform, and the cycle quietly stalls.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: Illuminated chloroplasts are treated so protons are no longer pumped into the thylakoid lumen and stromal pH stays near 7. Predict the effect on Rubisco activation, and why.
cards.back: Activation falls. Without the pH rise, Lys-201 reacts poorly with CO₂ to form the carbamate; in the textbook account the Mg²⁺ rise is also lost, so the carbamate–Mg²⁺ pair is less complete.
cards.why: In the textbook account, proton pumping raises stromal pH and Mg²⁺ moves into the stroma; both act on Rubisco.
cards.quote: Second, in the textbook account, Mg²⁺ flows out of the lumen into the stroma to balance the charge.
cards.section: Act 2: the control panel runs on light

cards.front: What are the products when Rubisco reacts RuBP with O₂ instead of CO₂?
cards.back: One 3-PGA plus one two-carbon phosphoglycolate. RuBP is spent and no carbon is fixed. This is photorespiration.
cards.quote: When O₂ wins the active site, RuBP is split into one 3-PGA plus one two-carbon phosphoglycolate
cards.section: Photorespiration: the ledger broken

cards.front: On a hot afternoon a C3 leaf closes its stomata to save water. Which Rubisco reaction gains, carboxylation or oxygenation, and why?
cards.back: Oxygenation. With stomata closed, CO₂ inside the leaf falls while O₂ stays high. Heat also lowers Rubisco's preference for CO₂ over O₂ and makes CO₂ less soluble relative to O₂.
cards.quote: With stomata closed, CO₂ inside the leaf falls while O₂ stays high.
cards.section: Photorespiration: the ledger broken

cards.front: Rubisco performs six oxygenations, using six RuBP (30 carbons). After salvage, is there enough carbon to rebuild all six RuBP?
cards.back: No. Oxygenation gives six 3-PGA (18 C) + six phosphoglycolates (12 C). Salvage turns the 12 C into three 3-PGA (9 C) + three CO₂. 18 + 9 = 27 C back, 30 needed: three carbons short.
cards.why: Salvage turns two phosphoglycolates (4 C) into one 3-PGA (3 C) plus one CO₂.
cards.quote: That is 27 carbons back and three lost as CO₂.
cards.section: Photorespiration: the ledger broken

cards.front: A crop carries a mutant Rubisco with a normal carboxylation rate but a lower preference for CO₂ over O₂. At constant light and temperature, how would raising the CO₂ concentration around Rubisco change its carbon budget?
cards.back: It would cut photorespiratory loss: CO₂ and O₂ compete for the same active site, so more CO₂ shifts Rubisco back toward carboxylation, sparing RuBP and the CO₂ released in salvage.
cards.why: This is the logic of C4 and CAM, which flood Rubisco with CO₂.
cards.quote: Malate is decarboxylated there, flooding Rubisco with CO₂.
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: Describe how C4 plants such as corn separate carbon capture from the Calvin cycle in space.
cards.back: In mesophyll cells, carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate and PEP carboxylase (no oxygenase activity) fixes it onto PEP → oxaloacetate → malate. Malate (some species use aspartate) moves to bundle-sheath cells and is decarboxylated, flooding Rubisco with CO₂.
cards.quote: In mesophyll cells, carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ into bicarbonate, and PEP carboxylase, which binds bicarbonate tightly and has no oxygenase activity, fixes it onto PEP to make oxaloacetate, then malate.
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: Regenerating PEP costs a maize-type C4 plant two extra ATP per CO₂. About how much ATP and NADPH does it spend per hexose, and how much more ATP is that than a C3 plant?
cards.back: Per CO₂: 3 + 2 = about 5 ATP + 2 NADPH. Per hexose (6 CO₂): about 30 ATP + 12 NADPH, about 12 ATP more than C3's 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.
cards.quote: Regenerating PEP costs two extra ATP per CO₂, so maize-type C4 runs at about 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: When do CAM plants (cacti, agave, pineapple) open their stomata, and what enzyme first fixes the CO₂?
cards.back: Mainly at night. PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into malate; by day, with stomata closed, the CO₂ is released to the Calvin cycle, conserving water.
cards.quote: they open stomata mainly at night and use the same PEP carboxylase to fix CO₂ into malate
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: A succulent stores malate overnight and keeps its stomata shut through midday; a second plant keeps stomata open by day and splits work between mesophyll and bundle-sheath cells. Name each strategy, the enzyme they share, and the trade-off.
cards.back: The first is CAM (separation in time, conserving water); the second is C4 (separation in space). Both make the first capture with PEP carboxylase. Both pay extra ATP, CAM usually somewhat more than C4.
cards.quote: CAM pays extra ATP too, usually somewhat more than C4
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: Relate photorespiration, C4 and CAM to the Calvin cycle's core count: each CO₂ uses one RuBP and makes two 3-PGA.
cards.back: Photorespiration spends RuBP without adding carbon, so the cost per net CO₂ rises. C4 and CAM spend extra ATP to pump CO₂ to Rubisco and suppress oxygenation.
cards.quote: Photorespiration spends RuBP without adding carbon; C4 and CAM pay ATP to suppress it.
cards.section: C4 and CAM: paying for a CO₂ pump

cards.front: Linear electron flow makes about 1.29 ATP per NADPH. What ATP:NADPH ratio does the C3 Calvin cycle need, and a maize-type C4 plant? How big is each shortfall?
cards.back: C3: 3/2 = 1.5, short by about 0.21 ATP per NADPH. C4: 5/2 = 2.5, short by about 1.21. Cyclic electron flow tops up the ATP.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's ratios (3 ATP + 2 NADPH; about 5 ATP + 2 NADPH) and its supply estimate.
cards.quote: linear electron flow makes about 1.29 ATP per NADPH, short of the 1.5 the cycle needs; cyclic electron flow tops up the ATP.
cards.section: Where the rule bends

cards.front: Outline Rubisco's carboxylation mechanism, from RuBP to two 3-PGA.
cards.back: RuBP forms a reactive 2,3-enediolate; CO₂ adds to C2, giving a six-carbon intermediate (2-carboxy-3-keto-arabinitol-1,5-bisphosphate) that is hydrated and cleaved between C2 and C3 into two 3-PGA.
cards.quote: CO₂ adds to C2, producing a six-carbon intermediate, 2-carboxy-3-keto-arabinitol-1,5-bisphosphate, that is immediately hydrated and cleaved between C2 and C3 into two 3-PGA.
cards.section: How Rubisco makes the cut

cards.front: Rubisco fixes one ¹⁴CO₂ onto unlabeled RuBP. How many of the two 3-PGA products carry the label, and in which group?
cards.back: One. The new carbon becomes that 3-PGA's carboxyl; the other 3-PGA is old RuBP carbon. That is why the bill is counted per 3-PGA, not per new atom.
cards.quote: Only one 3-PGA carries the new carbon, as its carboxyl; the other is old RuBP carbon
cards.section: How Rubisco makes the cut

cards.front: Why do C4 and C3 plants carry distinct carbon-isotope signatures?
cards.back: C4 plants make their first capture with PEP carboxylase, which discriminates much less against heavy ¹³C than Rubisco does. Paleoecologists read this fingerprint in fossils.
cards.quote: PEP carboxylase discriminates much less against heavy 13C than Rubisco does, which is why C4 and C3 plants carry distinct isotopic signatures
cards.section: C4 isotope signatures

cards.front: A volcanic haze scatters sunlight into diffuse light over a deciduous forest. Predict the effect on the canopy's photosynthesis on clear days, and why.
cards.back: It rises. The upper canopy was already light-saturated, so diffuse light reaching deeper into shaded lower leaves adds fixation there.
cards.why: Canopy fixation depends on how evenly light reaches leaves, not only on how much arrives.
cards.quote: the upper canopy was already light-saturated, so the diffuse light reached deeper into shaded lower leaves that had been starved for photons.
cards.section: Diffuse light and the Pinatubo canopy
